claim: cfDNA is believed to be generated largely by apoptotic cells.
source: Although cfDNA is believed to be generated largely by apoptotic cells (Grabuschnig et al., 2020), this phenomenon is not limited to cells undergoing a death pathway.
evidence: Supported by citation to Grabuschnig et al., 2020

claim: Active release of nucleic acids encapsulated in extracellular vesicles is a potential route for cfDNA release.
source: Active release of nucleic acids encapsulated in extracellular vesicles (Kustanovich et al., 2019) or through mitochondrial channels (Xian et al., 2022) are additional potential routes that may permit the release of cfDNA.
evidence: Supported by citation to Kustanovich et al., 2019

claim: Release through mitochondrial channels is a potential route for cfDNA release.

claim: Several measures including concentration, fragment size, sequence, and epigenetic modifications can be used to characterize cfDNA.
source: Several measures, including concentration, fragment size, sequence, and epigenetic modifications such as differential methylation, histone modification, and nucleosome spacing, can be used to characterize cfDNA and imply information about the cells from which it originated (Zukowski et al., 2020; Lehmann-Werman et al., 2016; Moss et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Zukowski et al., 2020; Lehmann-Werman et al., 2016; Moss et al., 2018

claim: cfDNA has diagnostic uses including noninvasive prenatal testing for chromosome abnormalities.
source: Currently, cfDNA already has some diagnostic uses, including noninvasive prenatal testing for chromosome abnormalities (Willems et al., 2014), fetal gender determination (Jacobsen et al., 2018), and cfDNA-based tests for the detection of mutations and cancer screening (Cisneros-Villanueva et al., 2022; Bronkhorst et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Willems et al., 2014

claim: cfDNA has diagnostic uses including fetal gender determination.

evidence: Supported by citation to Jacobsen et al., 2018

claim: cfDNA-based tests are used for the detection of mutations and cancer screening.

claim: The clinical utility and accuracy of cfDNA tests in the prediction of cancer is uncertain in some cases.
